solutionSteps: \textnormal{Define the Chebyshev polynomials by the recurrence. Their trigonometric identity follows by induction from the cosine addition formula.}

\textnormal{The polynomial minus one has exactly the roots in the sum. Interior cosine roots are double because the two angles give the same value; endpoint roots have their corresponding single multiplicities.}
\textnormal{Logarithmically differentiate this finite product. The evaluation point exceeds every root, so no denominator vanishes.}

analyticCertificate: T_n(cos theta)-1 vanishes at all displayed angles. At interior paired angles its first theta derivative vanishes and second does not, giving double roots in z; at theta=0 and, when relevant, pi the root in z is single. These multiplicities total n, and the leading coefficient gives the product constant.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For any positive parameter t, maximize a power times a decaying exponential to bound every nonnegative summand index.}
\textnormal{The logarithm of the resulting root bound is minimized when the parameter times its exponential equals the reciprocal of lambda.}
\textnormal{For the matching lower bound keep just the term at the integer part of N divided by this optimizing parameter. Its scaled index tends to the displayed positive limit.}
k_N=\left\lfloor\frac N{\frac{1}{2}}\right\rfloor,\qquad\frac{k_N}N\longrightarrow c=\frac1{\frac{1}{2}},\qquad S_N\ge e^{-\lambda N}\frac{k_N^N(\lambda N)^{k_N}}{k_N!}.
\textnormal{Take logarithms, divide by N, subtract the logarithm of N, and apply Stirling to the one factorial. The rounding error is lower order.}
\textnormal{The bounds agree because the chosen c satisfies c times the logarithm of c divided by lambda equals one.}

analyticCertificate: For fixed N the factorial series is absolutely convergent by the ratio test. The exponential majorant is derived by differentiating u^N exp(-tu), not by assuming a moment asymptotic. The explicit t solves the unique critical point of -ln t+lambda(e^t-1), whose second derivative is positive. Stirling at k_N~cN gives a matching single-term lower bound.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Repeated integration by parts with a beta polynomial gives an exact remainder, valid for every real z.}

\textnormal{At the moving positive argument, the nth root of the integral tends to the maximum of its continuous nonnegative base. This follows by bounding above by its maximum and below on any fixed small interval around a maximizer.}

\textnormal{The logarithmic derivative decreases strictly from positive infinity to negative infinity, so this is the unique global maximum. Stirling gives the remaining moving-argument normalization.}

analyticCertificate: The exact remainder follows by moving 2N+1 derivatives from the exponential onto t^N(1-t)^N; endpoint derivatives below N vanish and the final derivative is zero. The bounded-interval maximum principle needs only continuity and nonnegativity, and the unique maximum is positive. All roots in the explicit critical point are positive principal roots.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Use a finite geometric identity inside the integral. It is exact even though the infinite factorial expansion would diverge at every fixed positive x.}
\textnormal{Normalize the nonnegative weight to a probability density. Integration by parts gives its first two moments.}
\textnormal{Thus t divided by N tends to one in probability by Chebyshev. The reciprocal function is bounded by one over a and continuous, so its expectation tends to one over a plus one.}

analyticCertificate: Integrating each of finitely many polynomial terms uses integral t^k exp(-t)=k!, proved by integration by parts. Chebyshev gives E[(t/N-1)^2]=(N+2)/N^2 ->0. Boundedness and continuity give expectation convergence via splitting a small neighborhood and its complement. Stirling is an explicit analytic prerequisite; no numerical agreement is used as proof.

authoring.referencePurpose: Mathematical references only; no third-party problem adaptation.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Use reciprocal-square-root weights in both indices. Decreasing integral comparison bounds both the row and column sums by the same constant.}
\textnormal{Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the bilinear sum after inserting the reciprocal weight ratios into its two factors. The two displayed bounds then give the required upper constant.}

\textnormal{For sharpness take both sequences to be the reciprocal-square-root sequence through N. For indices j between a large fixed cutoff and N divided by that cutoff, the normalized inner sum approaches the full beta integral uniformly as the cutoff increases.}
\textnormal{Sum over these middle indices with weight one over j. Dividing by the harmonic sum through N and first sending N, then K, to infinity gives the matching lower constant.}
statement: \textnormal{Find the least constant C for which the inequality holds for all positive integers N and all real sequences of the indicated finite length.}\quad\left|\sum_{j,k=1}^{N}\frac{a_jb_k}{j+2k}\right|\le C\left(\sum_{j=1}^{N}a_j^2\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{N}b_k^2\right)^{1/2}.

analyticCertificate: All sums in the upper bound are finite, and the positive comparison integrals bound their extensions. For the sharp lower bound, a decreasing k-integrand has its sum at least its integral from 1 to N+1. After t=j u this contains [1/K,K] whenever K<=j<=N/K. The fraction of H_N in that middle logarithmic range tends to one for fixed K. The beta integral tends to pi/sqrt(m) as K increases. No symmetry of the asymmetric matrix is assumed.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Use reciprocal-square-root weights in both indices. Decreasing integral comparison bounds both the row and column sums by the same constant.}
\textnormal{Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the bilinear sum after inserting the reciprocal weight ratios into its two factors. The two displayed bounds then give the required upper constant.}

\textnormal{For sharpness take both sequences to be the reciprocal-square-root sequence through N. For indices j between a large fixed cutoff and N divided by that cutoff, the normalized inner sum approaches the full beta integral uniformly as the cutoff increases.}
\textnormal{Sum over these middle indices with weight one over j. Dividing by the harmonic sum through N and first sending N, then K, to infinity gives the matching lower constant.}
statement: \textnormal{Find the least constant C for which the inequality holds for all positive integers N and all real sequences of the indicated finite length.}\quad\left|\sum_{j,k=1}^{N}\frac{a_jb_k}{j+6k}\right|\le C\left(\sum_{j=1}^{N}a_j^2\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{N}b_k^2\right)^{1/2}.

analyticCertificate: All sums in the upper bound are finite, and the positive comparison integrals bound their extensions. For the sharp lower bound, a decreasing k-integrand has its sum at least its integral from 1 to N+1. After t=j u this contains [1/K,K] whenever K<=j<=N/K. The fraction of H_N in that middle logarithmic range tends to one for fixed K. The beta integral tends to pi/sqrt(m) as K increases. No symmetry of the asymmetric matrix is assumed.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Use positive auxiliary weights whose weighted products telescope. All exponents below use the same displayed weights.}
\textnormal{Weighted AM-GM applied to the products of c and a gives a summable upper bound.}
\textnormal{Reverse the nonnegative sums and simplify each resulting coefficient.}
\textnormal{For sharpness, take the reciprocal sequence through N and zero afterward. Polynomial-weight Riemann sums, with a controlled logarithmic endpoint, determine each weighted geometric mean.}
\textnormal{Consequently the ratio of the two finite sums tends to this exponential constant as N increases. Every truncated sequence is admissible, proving sharpness.}
statement: \textnormal{Find the least constant C for which this inequality holds for every nonnegative real sequence with finite sum. The weights and their partial sums are defined below.}\quad\lambda_k=\binom{k+0}{1},\quad\Lambda_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\lambda_k=\binom{n+1}{2},\quad\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\prod_{k=1}^{n}a_k^{\lambda_k/\Lambda_n}\le C\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}a_k.

analyticCertificate: The binomial hockey-stick identity gives Lambda. Weighted AM-GM is valid for nonnegative entries and positive weights. The displayed reciprocal-Lambda difference telescopes to the stated tail because Lambda tends to infinity. Lambda_n~n^m/m! and lambda_k~k^(m-1)/(m-1)! reduce the log correction to m integral_0^1 t^(m-1)ln t=-1/m; the endpoint contribution is uniformly controlled by an integrable logarithmic power, and lower polynomial terms are negligible. Zeros after N make all later weighted geometric means zero.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Let CT mean the coefficient of zero powers in all three Laurent variables. Pair opposite variable ratios in the following product.}
\textnormal{The three cyclic exponents agree exactly when the product term is constant, giving the displayed alternating sum for exponent sizes N, twice N, and the third displayed multiple of N.}

\textnormal{For positive integer exponents, the rational identity below gives the three-term decrement recurrence. At a zero exponent, the corresponding variable constant term reduces to the two-variable binomial identity.}
\textnormal{Apply Stirling to the four factorials. The exponential factor is canceled by the normalization in the question, leaving the square-root factor and one inverse power of N.}

analyticCertificate: The Good recurrence plus zero-exponent boundary values proves the factorial constant term by induction on total degree. The multinomial factorial expression obeys the same recurrence and boundaries. The two-dimensional Stirling prefactor is (2pi N)^-1 sqrt((m+3)/(2m)); no cancellation estimate based on numerical summation is used.

\textnormal{The tail cross-entropy on the right is no larger than the full tail cross-entropy, because every tail index is at least N plus one. The full cross-entropy is finite by the mean constraint.}

\textnormal{For a positive exponent p, every integer in the L-digit block lies between the corresponding consecutive powers of the base. Its whole block contribution is therefore bounded above and below by fixed multiples of the same geometric scale.}

\textnormal{The growing characteristic root determines convergence. At equality the block contributions stay bounded away from zero, so the boundary diverges. For nonpositive p the summands themselves cannot tend to zero.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Introduce a rational potential whose mixed forward difference is the given summand.}
\textnormal{For the first iterated order, let the inner n cutoff increase first; for the second order let the m cutoff increase first. On a square cutoff the first potential term is one half.}

\textnormal{Each individual row and column is absolutely summable, but the full absolute double sum diverges. On the wedge where n lies between one quarter and one half of m, the positive summand is bounded below by a constant times one over m squared; there are a number of such terms proportional to m. The resulting harmonic lower bound explains why changing order is not justified.}

For large m and m/4<=n<=m/2, numerator>=m/2 and denominator<=((3/2)m+2)^3, giving a uniform positive multiple of m^-2. The allowed n count is at least m/5 for large m, so the absolute double series dominates a harmonic tail.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Keep p equal to the exponent in the question, and define its conjugate ratio and a positive auxiliary sequence.}
\textnormal{The identity for the partial sums follows by induction. Holder bounds the numerator in each mean using these weights.}
\textnormal{Bernoulli’s inequality gives a telescoping upper bound for the coefficient tail.}
\textnormal{Reverse the nonnegative sums and telescope; the auxiliary sequence tends to zero, so the upper constant is c to the power p.}

\textnormal{For sharpness take }a_k\textnormal{ equal to k to the power minus one over p through N and zero afterward. Integral comparison gives the asymptotic size of every prefix mean, and the first N output terms already approach the upper ratio.}
statement: \textnormal{Find the least real C for which the inequality holds for every nonnegative sequence whose displayed power sum is finite.}\quad p=\frac{3}{2},\qquad\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{a_1+\cdots+a_n}{n}\right)^p\le C\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n^p.

analyticCertificate: With q=p-1>0 and x=1/(pn), (1-x)^(-q)>=1+qx implies the displayed tail inequality. The auxiliary sequence tends to zero because its logarithm is at most minus (1/p) times a divergent harmonic partial sum. Tonelli handles the nonnegative sum reversal. Every truncated sharpness sequence has finite p sum, and the integral comparison asymptotic yields the harmonic weighted-average limit. This shares the broad theme of sharp mean inequalities with Carleman, but the central power-space Holder operator estimate differs from weighted geometric AM-GM.

statement: \textnormal{Let }\Omega(n)\textnormal{ be the total number of prime factors of the positive integer }n\textnormal{ counted with multiplicity, with }\Omega(1)=0.\textnormal{ Define the zeta function by its convergent series.}\quad\Omega(12)=3,\qquad\zeta(s)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^{-s}\ (s>1).\quad\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{\Omega(n)}}{n^{2}}=?

analyticCertificate: Finite prime products sum precisely over integers supported on those primes. Absolute convergence lets the finite support restriction grow to all integers. solutionSteps: \textnormal{Keep p equal to the exponent in the question, and define its conjugate ratio and a positive auxiliary sequence.}
\textnormal{The identity for the partial sums follows by induction. Holder bounds the numerator in each mean using these weights.}
\textnormal{Bernoulli’s inequality gives a telescoping upper bound for the coefficient tail.}
\textnormal{Reverse the nonnegative sums and telescope; the auxiliary sequence tends to zero, so the upper constant is c to the power p.}

\textnormal{For sharpness take }a_k\textnormal{ equal to k to the power minus one over p through N and zero afterward. Integral comparison gives the asymptotic size of every prefix mean, and the first N output terms already approach the upper ratio.}
statement: \textnormal{Find the least real C for which the inequality holds for every nonnegative sequence whose displayed power sum is finite.}\quad p=\frac{4}{3},\qquad\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{a_1+\cdots+a_n}{n}\right)^p\le C\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n^p.

analyticCertificate: With q=p-1>0 and x=1/(pn), (1-x)^(-q)>=1+qx implies the displayed tail inequality. The auxiliary sequence tends to zero because its logarithm is at most minus (1/p) times a divergent harmonic partial sum. Tonelli handles the nonnegative sum reversal. Every truncated sharpness sequence has finite p sum, and the integral comparison asymptotic yields the harmonic weighted-average limit. This shares the broad theme of sharp mean inequalities with Carleman, but the central power-space Holder operator estimate differs from weighted geometric AM-GM.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{All entrywise geometric series converge, since their ratios lie strictly between zero and one.}

\textnormal{Multiply a determinant of this form by all its denominators. The result is a polynomial alternating in the row nodes and separately in the column nodes. It therefore contains both Vandermonde products.}

\textnormal{Each node has degree at most n minus one in the polynomial, exactly the degree of its Vandermonde factor. Thus the remaining factor C is a constant. To determine it, replace every row node by t times that node and expand about t equal to zero.}

\textnormal{Multilinearity makes any repeated exponent give a zero determinant. The first nonzero total degree uses precisely the exponents from zero through n minus one. Its coefficient is the product of the two Vandermonde determinants. The denominator product has constant term one, so C equals one.}
\textnormal{Now extract the powers of q from each pair. A difference of indices d occurs n minus d times.}
statement: n=5,\quad q=\frac1{2},\qquad M_{ij}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}q^{(i+j+1)k}\quad(0\le i,j<n).\quad \textnormal{Here M is the square matrix with these entries. Find the displayed normalized determinant.}\quad\frac{\det(M)\displaystyle\prod_{i,j=0}^{n-1}(1-q^{i+j+1})}{\displaystyle\prod_{d=1}^{n-1}(1-q^d)^{2(n-d)}}.

analyticCertificate: The matrix and every product are finite, and no denominator vanishes since 0<q<1. Multiplying the determinant by its full denominator clears fractions. Alternation forces each pairwise difference divisor; the individual node degree bound leaves only a constant. The local analytic expansion near t=0 is valid uniformly over finitely many nodes. Multilinearity or finite Cauchy-Binet computes its first nonzero coefficient from exponents0 through n-1, fixing the constant as1. This finite polynomial identity then holds wherever its displayed rational denominators are nonzero.

\textnormal{Multiply a determinant of this form by all its denominators. The result is a polynomial alternating in the row nodes and separately in the column nodes. It therefore contains both Vandermonde products.}

\textnormal{Each node has degree at most n minus one in the polynomial, exactly the degree of its Vandermonde factor. Thus the remaining factor C is a constant. To determine it, replace every row node by t times that node and expand about t equal to zero.}

\textnormal{Multilinearity makes any repeated exponent give a zero determinant. The first nonzero total degree uses precisely the exponents from zero through n minus one. Its coefficient is the product of the two Vandermonde determinants. The denominator product has constant term one, so C equals one.}
\textnormal{Now extract the powers of q from each pair. A difference of indices d occurs n minus d times.}
statement: n=7,\quad q=\frac1{3},\qquad M_{ij}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}q^{(i+j+1)k}\quad(0\le i,j<n).\quad \textnormal{Here M is the square matrix with these entries. Find the displayed normalized determinant.}\quad\frac{\det(M)\displaystyle\prod_{i,j=0}^{n-1}(1-q^{i+j+1})}{\displaystyle\prod_{d=1}^{n-1}(1-q^d)^{2(n-d)}}.

Alternation forces each pairwise difference divisor; the individual node degree bound leaves only a constant. The local analytic expansion near t=0 is valid uniformly over finitely many nodes. Multilinearity or finite Cauchy-Binet computes its first nonzero coefficient from exponents0 through n-1, fixing the constant as1. This finite polynomial identity then holds wherever its displayed rational denominators are nonzero.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Let }S_M\textnormal{ denote the first M terms of the unweighted alternating logarithmic series. Pairing terms and using the Gamma recurrence gives a finite identity.}
\textnormal{The adjacent odd partial sum includes one additional positive logarithm. Averaging the neighboring even and odd partial sums cancels their growing logarithms.}
\textnormal{Therefore the averages of all partial sums tend to this same value. A second summation-by-parts identity turns those Cesaro averages into the requested Abel limit.}

\textnormal{The nonnegative weights on the right sum to one, and every fixed initial segment has total weight tending to zero. Since the Cesaro averages converge, their weighted average has the same limit.}
